title: The Quiet Skill That Gets Africans Hired Abroad
excerpt: It is not confidence and it is not your accent. It is whether anyone can see how you think.
content:
I have watched brilliant people get passed over for roles they were clearly qualified for, and I have watched less capable people sail through. For a long time I put it down to luck, or connections, or the unfairness people warn you about. Some of it is. But a large part of it is a skill nobody teaches, and most people do not realise they are being assessed on.

It is not confidence. It is not your accent. It is the ability to make your thinking visible.

Where the gap comes from

Many of us were trained, at school and at work, that the right answer speaks for itself. You do the work, you present the result, and the quality is obvious. Explaining your reasoning too much can look like you are unsure, or worse, like you are showing off.

That instinct serves you badly in a global team, and it serves you terribly in a remote one.

When your manager sits three thousand miles away and has never watched you work, the result on its own tells them very little. They cannot see the four options you considered, the risk you spotted, or the shortcut you deliberately refused to take. All of that judgement, which is the actual thing they are paying for, stays invisible. What reaches them is a finished file and silence.

Meanwhile a colleague who did more ordinary work, but narrated it clearly along the way, reads as more senior. Not because they performed better, but because their thinking was legible and yours was not.

What making thinking visible looks like

It is smaller and less dramatic than people expect. Mostly it is a few extra sentences attached to work you were already doing.

Instead of sending the finished report with the message Please find attached, you send it with three lines. What you were asked for. What you found. What you think should happen next, and why. Thirty seconds of writing, and the reader now knows they are dealing with someone who thinks, not someone who types.

Instead of going quiet for four days on a difficult task, you post a short note on day two saying where you have got to and what is slowing you down. Silence during difficulty reads as struggling. A brief honest update reads as control.

Instead of answering a question with only the answer, you give the answer and the reason underneath it. Yes, roughly two weeks, because the data cleanup is the slow part and I would rather not rush that. Now your estimate is something they can push on, and you look like a partner rather than a service desk.

In interviews, this is the whole game

Interviewers ask about a difficult project not because they care about the project. They care about how you decide things under pressure, and the project is simply the excuse to watch you do it.

So when you answer, do not just tell them what happened. Tell them what you were weighing.

  • What the situation actually was, briefly.
  • What the options were, including the one you rejected.
  • Why you chose the one you chose.
  • What happened, including what you would do differently.

That third point is where most people go quiet, and it is the one carrying nearly all the signal. Anyone can describe a decision. Describing the trade off shows you understood there was one.

A note on humility

There is a real cultural tension here, and it is worth naming honestly. In much of West Africa, talking at length about your own reasoning can feel immodest. There is a strong value placed on letting the work speak.

But notice what is actually being asked. Nobody is telling you to boast. Explaining why you chose one approach over another is not self promotion. It is information the other person needs in order to trust you with something bigger. Withholding it is not modesty. It is, unintentionally, making your colleague guess.

You can stay entirely humble and still be clear. The two were never in conflict.

Start this week

Pick one thing you are working on. Before you hand it over, write three sentences: what you were solving, what you decided, and why. Attach them.

Do that for a month and something shifts. People start bringing you into decisions earlier. The work you get asked to do changes shape. None of your actual ability changed. It just became possible to see from the outside.
author: Fisayo Adeyemi
